title: EDA
text:
Click here for information about the data we will be analyzing. A summary has been given below.


“Access to safe drinking-water is essential to health, a basic human right and a component of effective policy for health protection. This is important as a health and development issue at a national, regional and local level.”




pH value: PH is an important parameter in evaluating the acid–base balance of water
Hardness: Hardness is mainly caused by calcium and magnesium salts.
Solids (Total dissolved solids - TDS): A wide range of inorganic and some organic minerals or salts such as potassium, calcium, sodium, bicarbonates, chlorides, magnesium, sulfates etc can be produced giving un-wanted taste and diluted color.
Chloramines: Chlorine and chloramine are the major disinfectants used in public water systems
Sulfate: Sulfates are naturally occurring substances that are found in minerals, soil, and rocks
Conductivity: Pure water is not a good conductor of electric current but rather is a good insulator.
Organic_carbon: Total Organic Carbon (TOC) in source waters comes from decaying natural organic matter (NOM) as well as synthetic sources.
Trihalomethanes: THMs are chemicals which may be found in water treated with chlorine.
Turbidity: The turbidity of water depends on the quantity of solid matter present in the suspended state.
Potability: Indicates if water is safe for human consumption




First we will read in the data. Since we know that Potability is our only categorical variable - and only has values of 0 and 1 - we will make it a factor variable. This will help us by giving us the text on if the water is potable or not instead of having to remember what a 0 or a 1 meant.

water_data_raw <- read_csv("Data/water_potability.csv") |>
  mutate(Potability = factor(Potability,
                             levels = c(0, 1),
                             labels = c("Not Potable", "Potable")))

The only noteworthy pieces of info at this point is that n is different for some of the variables due to the presence of NA entries. Also, not that it will mean much to us, but due to changing Potability to a factor variable, the values are now counted as 1s and 2s instead of 0s and 1s. This is why our mean is allowed to be greater than 1, despite the variable only being coded as 0s and 1s originally. Since Potability is considered a categorical variable, we do not need these summary statistics of it, but at first glance it appears that the data would have been entered or read incorrectly. After dropping all NA observations, we still have over 2000 data observations. This should be more than plenty. If it is found that three variables with NA entries are not important to our models, we can add back in the removed data and recalculate the models, if need be.



Potability will be used as our response variable for our model fitting. We will group by Potability status for our summary.

  summarize(count = n())

Out of our 2011 observations, 1200 were Not Potable water and 811 were Potable.

  group_by(Potability) |>
  summarize(mean_ph = mean(ph),

It appears that Potable water had a slightly higher mean and median pH than Not Potable water. However, the values are fairly close with standard deviations that might lead us to believe that they are not statistically significant. That is not our purpose in this study, but it could warrant further study.

Now that we have the summary information about each variable, we can see that there is not much difference between the Potable and Not Potable water. A further, deeper T-test could tell us if any of these values are statistically significant (again, not our purpose). However, on quick glance, there does seem to be any obviously significant differences for us to focus on.




water_data |>
  pivot_longer(
    cols = c(ph, Hardness, Solids, Chloramines, Sulfate,
             Conductivity, Organic_carbon,
             Trihalomethanes, Turbidity),
    names_to = "Variable",
    values_to = "Value"
  ) |>
  ggplot(aes(x = Value, fill = Potability)) +
  geom_density(alpha = 0.5) +
  facet_wrap(~ Variable, scales = "free") +
  labs(
    title = "Density Plots of Variables by Potability",
    x = "Value",
    y = "Density",
    fill = "Potability"
  )








This is backed up by the graphs above. Each density plot is grouped by Potability status. Many of the variables have a similar distribution for each Potability status. Sulfate, pH, and hardness seem to be the three variables with the most notable differences. However, the distributions have similar center values, but different spreads. Initial intuition would have guessed that the centers might also be different leading to a change in Potability status. That does not appear to be the case.

Since there is not any obvious signs from a signal variable to influence Potability status, maybe there is a connection between two variables. The above correlation matrix shows that there is not a strong correlation between any variables. The strongest magnitude correlation is between Sulfate and Solids at r = -0.163. This is still a weak correlation, and most of the other r values are less than 0.02 in magnitude.

water_data |>
  pivot_longer(
    cols = c(Hardness, Solids, Chloramines, Sulfate,
             Conductivity, Organic_carbon,
             Trihalomethanes, Turbidity),
    names_to = "Variable",
    values_to = "Value"
  ) |>
  ggplot(aes(x = ph, y = Value, color = Potability)) +
  geom_point(alpha = 0.4) +
  geom_smooth(method = "lm", se = FALSE) +
  facet_wrap(~ Variable, scales = "free_y") +
  labs(
    title = "Relationship Between pH and Other Variables",
    x = "pH",
    y = "Value",
    color = "Potability"
  )

`geom_smooth()` using formula = 'y ~ x'









These graphs show the relationship between pH and all other numeric variables. The strongest correlation between these is pH vs. Hardness at r = 0.103. Every scatter plot shows mostly a random scatter of points.
Because the other variables have similar correlation values, it stands to reason that the scatter plots of other variables on the x-axis would yield similar graphs.
There does not appear to be a single or pair of variables that would accurately predict the potability of water. We will need to create a model that incorporates many (if not all) of these variables to predict Potability.

text:
water_data <- read_csv("Data/water_potability.csv") |>
  mutate(Potability = factor(Potability,
                             levels = c(0, 1),
                             labels = c("Not Potable", "Potable"))) |>
  drop_na()

set.seed(123)

water_split <- initial_split(
  water_data,
  prop = 0.70,
  strata = Potability
)

water_train <- training(water_split)
water_test  <- testing(water_split)


water_test |>
  group_by(Potability) |>
  summarize(count = n()) |>
  mutate(proportion = count / sum(count))

# A tibble: 2 × 3
  Potability  count proportion
  <fct>       <int>      <dbl>
1 Not Potable   360      0.596
2 Potable       244      0.404



water_train |>
  group_by(Potability) |>
  summarize(count = n()) |>
  mutate(proportion = count / sum(count))

# A tibble: 2 × 3
  Potability  count proportion
  <fct>       <int>      <dbl>
1 Not Potable   840      0.597
2 Potable       567      0.403



water_folds <- vfold_cv(
  water_train,
  v = 5,
  strata = Potability
)


water_recipe <-
  recipe(Potability ~ ., data = water_train)


Classification Tree Explanation

A classification tree is a supervised learning algorithm used when the response variable is categorical. The algorithm recursively partitions the predictor space by selecting variables and split points that best separate the classes. Beginning at the root node, observations are divided into increasingly homogeneous groups until a stopping criterion is met. Each terminal node predicts the class that is most common among the training observations in that region.
One of the main tuning parameters is the complexity parameter (cost complexity). Larger values produce smaller, simpler trees by penalizing additional splits, while smaller values allow more complex trees that may better fit the training data but increase the risk of overfitting. Cross-validation is used to identify the complexity parameter that provides the best balance between model complexity and predictive performance.

tree_model <-
  decision_tree(
    cost_complexity = tune(),
    mode = "classification"
  ) |>
  set_engine("rpart")


tree_workflow <-
  workflow() |>
  add_recipe(water_recipe) |>
  add_model(tree_model)


tree_grid <-
  tibble(
    cost_complexity = 10^seq(-5, -1, length.out = 20)
  )


tree_results <-
  tune_grid(
    tree_workflow,
    resamples = water_folds,
    grid = tree_grid,
    metrics = metric_set(mn_log_loss)
  )


collect_metrics(tree_results) |>
  arrange(mean)

Random Forest Explanation

A random forest is an ensemble learning method that builds upon the basic classification tree. Instead of constructing a single tree, a random forest grows hundreds of decision trees using bootstrap samples of the training data. At each split, only a random subset of predictors is considered, increasing diversity among the trees. Final predictions are obtained by combining the predictions from all trees through majority voting.
Because individual trees are highly variable, averaging many trees substantially reduces prediction variance while maintaining low bias. This generally results in better predictive performance and greater resistance to overfitting than a single classification tree.
The primary tuning parameter considered here is mtry, which controls the number of randomly selected predictors considered at each split.

rf_model <-
  rand_forest(
    mtry = tune(),
    trees = 500,
    mode = "classification"
  ) |>
  set_engine("ranger")


rf_workflow <-
  workflow() |>
  add_recipe(water_recipe) |>
  add_model(rf_model)


rf_grid <- tibble(mtry = 1:9)


rf_results <-
  tune_grid(
    rf_workflow,
    resamples = water_folds,
    grid = rf_grid,
    metrics = metric_set(mn_log_loss)
  )

collect_metrics(rf_results) |>
  arrange(mean)

                y = mean, 
                text = hover_text)) +
  geom_errorbar(
    aes(ymin = mean - std_err, ymax = mean + std_err),
    width = 0.2,
    color = "black"
  ) +
  geom_line(color = "lightblue", group = 1) +
  geom_point(color = "blue", size = 3) +
  labs(
    title = "Random Forest Tuning Results",
    x = "mtry",
    y = "Mean Log Loss"
  )

ggplotly(q, tooltip = "text")






best_rf <- select_best(rf_results, metric = "mn_log_loss")

final_rf <- finalize_workflow(rf_workflow, best_rf)


tree_fit <-fit(final_tree, data = water_train)

rf_fit <-fit(final_rf, data = water_train)


tree_last_fit <-
  last_fit(
    final_tree,
    split = water_split,
    metrics = metric_set(mn_log_loss)
  )

collect_metrics(tree_last_fit)

# A tibble: 1 × 4
  .metric     .estimator .estimate .config        
  <chr>       <chr>          <dbl> <chr>          
1 mn_log_loss binary         0.682 pre0_mod0_post0



rf_last_fit <-
  last_fit(
    final_rf,
    split = water_split,
    metrics = metric_set(mn_log_loss)
  )

collect_metrics(rf_last_fit)

# A tibble: 1 × 4
  .metric     .estimator .estimate .config        
  <chr>       <chr>          <dbl> <chr>          
1 mn_log_loss binary         0.602 pre0_mod0_post0


The classification tree and random forest models were both tuned using five-fold cross-validation with multinomial log-loss as the evaluation metric. On the independent test set, the classification tree achieved a log-loss of 0.682, while the random forest achieved a lower log-loss of 0.602. Because lower log-loss indicates better predictions, the random forest outperformed the classification tree. This result is consistent with the cross-validation results, where the random forest also achieved the lowest average log-loss, suggesting that aggregating predictions across many decision trees produced better generalization than a single classification tree.
